title: AI Meets the Classroom: When Do Large Language Models Harm Learning?
extended_summary:
This paper investigates when large language models (LLMs) help or harm student learning, addressing mixed prior evidence about whether tools like ChatGPT improve educational outcomes or undermine them. The authors conceptualize learning as involving both the volume of topics covered and the depth of understanding of each topic, and ask whether LLM access changes either or both. They study unrestricted LLM use rather than tightly constrained tutoring systems, with a particular focus on coding education.

The paper reports three empirical studies: a field study of two graduate programming courses and two pre-registered, incentivized laboratory experiments in which students learned introductory Python. In the field study, the authors use similarity between student code and ChatGPT-generated code, along with variation from ChatGPT outages, to estimate the effects of substitutive LLM use during coursework. In the lab studies, participants were randomly assigned to have or not have LLM access during the learning phase; Study 3 additionally enabled copy-and-paste, which changed how participants used the model. The authors also manually coded LLM chat logs to distinguish substitutive use (asking for solutions) from complementary use (asking for explanations).

The populations were students in Europe: graduate students in two programming courses at a Dutch public university and student participants from a German university laboratory pool, most with little or no prior Python experience. The field context involved course assignments over 4-5 weeks, while the lab context involved short Python learning sessions with pre-tests, a 45-minute learning phase, and post-tests completed in a single session.

The main conclusion is that LLMs had no overall effect on learning outcomes in the two randomized lab experiments, but their effects depended strongly on usage behavior. Substitutive use let students move faster and cover more topics, but reduced understanding of each topic and in the field study was associated with worse later performance. Complementary use, such as requesting explanations, improved understanding but did not increase topic volume. The paper also finds heterogeneous effects by prior knowledge: students with higher prior knowledge benefited more, while those with lower prior knowledge were harmed, suggesting that LLMs may widen educational inequality. Finally, LLM access increased perceived learning more than actual learning gains justified.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s large language model chatbot used as a general-purpose conversational assistant with coding and explanation capabilities.
identified_tools.use_case: Students used ChatGPT while learning introductory Python programming and in field-course homework contexts, either to generate coding solutions (substitutive use) or to provide explanations/tutoring (complementary use). The paper also used ChatGPT-generated code to proxy student AI use in the field study.

findings.finding_summary: In the field study of two graduate programming courses, cumulative ChatGPT similarity was negatively associated with subsequent assignment performance in a two-way fixed effects model: if students submitted code identical to a ChatGPT-generated solution, their grade on all subsequent questions decreased by 0.02 (p<0.001). In the FE2SLS specification using ChatGPT outages as instruments, the negative cumulative effect remained and increased in magnitude to -0.06 (p=0.002), indicating worse later performance from substitutive use.
findings.measure: Normalized grade on subsequent programming questions in course assignments

findings.finding_summary: For current-question performance in the field study, ChatGPT similarity had a positive significant association in the FE model, increasing the current question grade by 0.18 (p<0.001), but this effect was not significant in the FE2SLS model (coefficient -0.35, p=0.334). This suggests any immediate gain on the focal question was not robust once using outage-based instrumental variables.
findings.measure: Normalized grade on current programming question

findings.finding_summary: In laboratory Study 2, access to ChatGPT during the learning phase did not significantly improve overall learning outcomes. The treatment effect on post-test performance was 0.396 (p=0.580) after adjusting for covariates, and the raw treatment-control post-test difference of about 1 question was also not significant (p=0.206).
findings.measure: Post-test number of correctly answered Python programming questions

findings.finding_summary: In laboratory Study 2, ChatGPT access did not significantly affect topic understanding after controlling for progress through the learning materials. In the regression including Learning Phase performance, the treatment effect on post-test scores was -0.276 (p=0.562).
findings.measure: Post-test correct answers controlling for Learning Phase progress (proxy for topic understanding)

findings.finding_summary: In laboratory Study 2, ChatGPT access did not significantly increase the volume of topics covered during the learning phase. The treatment effect on the number of correctly answered learning-phase questions was 0.828 (p=0.214).

In laboratory Study 3, where copy-and-paste was enabled, ChatGPT access still did not significantly improve overall learning outcomes after covariate adjustment. The treatment effect on post-test score was 0.959 (p=0.298), although the raw post-test difference was about 2 questions and marginal in a Welch’s t-test (p=0.092).
findings.measure: Post-test number of correctly answered Python programming questions

findings.finding_summary: In laboratory Study 3, ChatGPT access significantly increased the volume of topics students covered during learning when copy-and-paste was available. The treatment effect on Learning Phase performance was 2.614 (p=0.013), and the raw treatment-control difference was about 4 questions (p=0.003).

In laboratory Study 3, ChatGPT access did not significantly affect topic understanding after accounting for learning-phase progress. The treatment effect on post-test performance controlling for Learning Phase was -0.651 (p=0.359).
findings.measure: Post-test correct answers controlling for Learning Phase progress (proxy for topic understanding)

findings.finding_summary: Across the combined experimental analyses, substitutive ChatGPT use increased topic volume but reduced understanding. Enabling copy-and-paste among treated students increased Learning Phase progress by 1.733 (p=0.033) but decreased post-test performance conditional on progress by -1.407 (p=0.009), while not affecting overall post-test scores (-0.249, p=0.737).
findings.measure: Learning Phase correct answers; post-test controlling for Learning Phase; overall post-test
findings.sample_size: n=94 treated subjects from Studies 2 and 3

findings.finding_summary: Message-level usage analyses showed that asking ChatGPT for solutions was associated with worse understanding, whereas asking for explanations was associated with better understanding. In regressions among treated students, Solutions predicted lower overall post-test performance marginally (-0.195, p<0.1) and lower post-test performance controlling for Learning Phase (-0.312, p<0.01), while Explanations did not predict overall post-test performance (-0.003, p=0.990) but positively predicted post-test performance controlling for Learning Phase (0.249, p=0.05).
findings.measure: Post-test correct answers; post-test correct answers controlling for Learning Phase
findings.sample_size: n=94 treated subjects from Studies 2 and 3

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT widened achievement gaps by prior knowledge in the combined experiments. The interaction of Treatment × Pre-test > Median was positive for overall post-test performance (2.528, p=0.028) and for understanding measured via post-test conditional on Learning Phase (1.613, p=0.034), while lower pre-test students in treatment understood significantly less than controls because the Treatment main effect on understanding was -0.950 (p=0.043).
findings.measure: Post-test correct answers; post-test correct answers controlling for Learning Phase; heterogeneity by pre-test median split
findings.effect_size: 2.528; 1.613; Treatment main effect for lower-knowledge students: -0.950

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT increased students’ perceived learning beyond what could be explained by actual learning gains. In the combined sample, Treatment increased Perceived Learning by 0.338 (p=0.044), and the effect remained 0.348 (p=0.043) when controlling for Learning Phase progress.
findings.measure: Self-reported perceived learning on a five-point Likert scale

quality_tier_rationale: The paper reports a field quasi-experimental study plus two pre-registered incentivized laboratory experiments with random assignment, but many core conclusions rely on exploratory analyses and some main treatment effects are null or context-dependent rather than clean RCT impacts.
impact_tier_rationale: Overall effects on learning are mostly null, but there are meaningful mixed subgroup and usage-pattern effects, including negative downstream performance from substitutive use and positive perceived learning. The practical impact is therefore unclear and highly contingent on how ChatGPT is used.
